title: MISRA-C & ISO 26262 Coding Standards: Static Analysis, Undefined Behavior & Safe Embedded Patterns
goal: Write mission-critical firmware worthy of automotive (ISO 26262 ASIL-D) and medical certification: eliminate Undefined Behavior (UB), enforce MISRA-C:2012 guidelines, and integrate static analysis linters.
recap: Yesterday we engineered tickless low-power sleep and watchdog supervision. Today we explore the world of functional safety and compliance: mastering the strict coding standards required for life-critical embedded systems.

parts.title: Functional Safety Standards & The Horrors of Undefined Behavior
say: The C programming language was designed for maximum efficiency and hardware closeness, not safety. As a result, the C ISO specification contains hundreds of instances of Undefined Behavior (UB), Implementation-Defined Behavior, and Unspecified Behavior.
In desktop software, undefined behavior might cause a program crash. In an electric vehicle's steer-by-wire controller or an insulin pump, undefined behavior can kill human beings.

To guarantee deterministic execution, safety standards such as ISO 26262 (Automotive ASIL A through D), DO-178C (Aerospace Flight Software), and IEC 61508 (Industrial Safety) mandate strict coding rules.

The worldwide gold standard for safety-critical C code is MISRA-C (Motor Industry Software Reliability Association). MISRA-C:2012 defines mandatory and required rules designed to eliminate language vulnerabilities before compilation.
parts.example: Signed integer overflow in C is undefined behavior. An optimizing compiler (GCC -O3) can legally assume that signed overflow never occurs, silently deleting critical safety limit checks from the binary!
parts.output:
--- DAY 28 PART 1: UNDEFINED BEHAVIOR & SAFETY STANDARDS ---
[UB-ANALYSIS] Testing Sensor Safety Check with input: 1000
  -> [SAFE] Sensor value within safe non-overflowing operating range.
[UB-ANALYSIS] Testing Sensor Safety Check with input: 2147483597
  -> [DANGER] Input rejected: Value exceeds safe arithmetic bounds.

codeNotes.note: Demonstrates why safety bounds must be checked using subtraction against MAX rather than testing after overflow.
In standard C, checking '(x + 1) < x' is undefined behavior for signed integers and optimized away by GCC/Clang.
MISRA-C requires defensive precondition validation before arithmetic operations take place.

parts.tryIt: Demonstrate unsigned wraparound: explain why unsigned integer arithmetic in C is defined (modulo 2^N) while signed arithmetic is undefined.

check.question: Why can an optimizing C compiler legally remove the safety check 'if (val + 100 < val) alert();' when 'val' is a signed 32-bit integer?
options: Under the C ISO standard, signed integer overflow is Undefined Behavior; the compiler assumes UB never happens and optimizes the check away as dead code.
The ARM architecture does not have an addition instruction.
The compiler only checks numbers smaller than 10.
Signed integers cannot be compared using the '<' operator in C99.
check.why: Because signed integer overflow is explicitly undefined in the C standard, the compiler's optimizer assumes valid C code will never trigger it. Since 'val + 100 < val' is mathematically false for all real numbers without overflow, the optimizer eliminates the check entirely.

parts.title: Essential Types & Implicit Promotion Hazards (Rule 10.4)
say: One of the most dangerous, subtle traps in C is the Integer Promotion Rule. In standard C, any integer type smaller than an 'int' (such as uint8_t and uint16_t) is automatically and silently promoted to a signed 'int' before any arithmetic operation.

Consider: uint16_t a = 40000; uint16_t b = 40000; uint32_t c = a + b; On a 32-bit microcontroller where 'int' is 32 bits, a and b are promoted to signed int, added to produce 80000, and converted to uint32_t.
However, if bitwise shifts are involved: uint16_t mask = 0x8000; uint32_t val = mask << 1; Here, mask is promoted to signed int. Shifting a 1 into the sign bit is undefined behavior!

MISRA-C Rule 10.4 introduces the concept of Essential Types, requiring that all operands in an expression share the exact same essential type and requiring explicit unsigned literals (such as 100U instead of 100).
parts.example: Writing 'uint8_t x = ~0x01;' causes 0x01 to be promoted to signed 32-bit int, inverted to 0xFFFFFFFE, and truncated back to uint8_t. MISRA-C requires 'uint8_t x = (uint8_t)~((uint8_t)0x01U);'.
parts.output:
--- DAY 28 PART 2: ESSENTIAL TYPES & PROMOTION HAZARDS ---
[MISRA-RULE-10.4] Essential Type Arithmetic:
  Operand A (uint16_t): 50000
  Operand B (uint16_t): 20000
  Compliant Result (uint32_t): 70000
  Safe Unsigned Mask (1U << 15): 0x8000

codeNotes.note: Always append the 'U' suffix to unsigned numeric literals (50000U) to comply with MISRA Rule 7.2.
Explicitly casts uint16_t operands to uint32_t before addition to prevent signed integer promotion.
Shifting literals must always be done on unsigned types (1U) to eliminate signed bit-shift undefined behavior.

parts.tryIt: Explain why MISRA-C bans the use of plain 'char' for arithmetic and mandates explicit 'uint8_t' or 'int8_t'.

check.question: Why does MISRA-C:2012 Rule 7.2 mandate appending the 'U' suffix to all unsigned integer constants (e.g., 500U)?
options: To explicitly force the compiler to treat the literal as unsigned, preventing implicit promotion to signed int and signed overflow UB.
To instruct the CPU hardware to store the number in the Ultra-fast cache register.
Because ARM Cortex-M assembler rejects numbers without letters.
To enable floating-point coprocessor acceleration.
check.why: Without the 'U' suffix, integer constants in C are signed integers by default. Operating with signed constants risks implicit signed promotions and signed overflow, which triggers undefined behavior.

parts.title: Bounded Loops & Banning Recursion (Rule 17.2)
say: In desktop computing, recursive algorithms (such as recursive quicksort or tree traversals) are common. In safety-critical embedded systems, recursion is strictly forbidden.
MISRA-C Rule 17.2 states: 'Functions shall not call themselves, either directly or indirectly.'

The engineering reason is stack determinism. Microcontrollers have fixed SRAM stack sizes. In recursive code, the maximum stack depth is dependent on runtime data and cannot be mathematically proven by static analysis tools at compile time.

Similarly, all loops (for, while) must have a provable upper bound. An unconstrained while loop waiting for a hardware flag can freeze the entire system if a trace on the PCB breaks. Every loop must incorporate a finite timeout counter.
parts.example: A while loop waiting for an ADC conversion flag must be bounded: 'uint32_t timeout = 10000U; while ((ADC->SR & EOC) == 0) { if (--timeout == 0U) return ERR_TIMEOUT; }'.
parts.output:
--- DAY 28 PART 3: BOUNDED LOOPS & RECURSION BAN ---
[MISRA-BOUNDS] Polling hardware register with upper bound: 100 iterations
  -> [SUCCESS] Hardware responded normally with 94 iterations remaining.
[MISRA-BOUNDS] Polling hardware register with upper bound: 100 iterations
  -> [TIMEOUT-TRIGGERED] Hardware failed to respond within bound! Aborting safely.

codeNotes.note: DriverStatus enum provides explicit deterministic return codes rather than crashing or freezing.
Bounded while loop: the loop is mathematically guaranteed to terminate after maxIterations cycles.
Defensive timeout abort prevents permanent CPU hang if a peripheral hardware line disconnects.

parts.tryIt: Convert an iterative factorial or binary search function to prove that it uses O(1) stack space compared to a recursive implementation.

check.question: Why does MISRA-C:2012 Rule 17.2 strictly forbid recursion in safety-critical firmware?
options: Because recursive stack growth cannot be mathematically proven or bounded at compile time, creating an unacceptable risk of stack overflow.
Because ARM Cortex-M processors do not possess a stack pointer register.
Because recursive functions cannot return values.
Because recursion disables all hardware interrupts.
check.why: In embedded microcontrollers with scarce, fixed SRAM stacks, recursive calls consume stack frames dynamically based on input data. Static analysis tools cannot verify that stack exhaustion will never occur, making recursion unacceptable for ASIL-D or DO-178C certification.

parts.title: Pointer Safety & Type Casting Invariants (Rules 11.4 & 21.3)
say: Pointer manipulation in C is a primary source of memory corruption. MISRA-C enforces strict pointer discipline.

Rule 11.4 forbids converting a pointer to an object type into a pointer to a different object type (e.g., casting a float* to a uint32_t* to inspect IEEE 754 bits). This violates strict aliasing and can cause compiler optimizations to misorder reads and writes.
Rule 21.3 strictly prohibits the use of dynamic memory allocation: malloc(), calloc(), realloc(), and free() from stdlib.h shall not be used.

Additionally, Rule 11.1 prohibits casting function pointers to void* or data pointers, and Rule 17.4 prohibits pointer arithmetic (array indexing a[i] must be used instead of *(a + i) for verifiable boundary checking).
parts.example: To inspect the raw byte representation of a float safely under MISRA, use a union or memcpy: 'memcpy(&rawBits, &floatVal, sizeof(rawBits));' rather than dangerous pointer aliasing.
parts.output:
--- DAY 28 PART 4: POINTER SAFETY & TYPE CASTING ---
[SAFE-PUNNING] Float Value: 3.14159
  Raw IEEE 754 Hex: 0x40490fd0

codeNotes.note: static_assert verifies compile-time size parity, ensuring memory copy operations are completely bounded.
std::memcpy is compliant with strict aliasing rules, unlike direct pointer cast punning (*(uint32_t*)&val).
Accurately extracts IEEE 754 single-precision bits without invoking undefined type punning behavior.

parts.tryIt: Explain why accessing an array using indexing 'buffer[index]' is safer for static analysis than pointer arithmetic '*(buffer + index)'.

check.question: Why does MISRA-C Rule 11.4 forbid casting a pointer to an object of one type into a pointer to a different object type (pointer punning)?
options: It violates strict aliasing rules, which allows optimizing compilers to reorder or delete reads and writes assuming pointers cannot alias.
The ARM bus matrix only allows pointers to be 8 bits wide.
Pointer casting disables the microcontroller floating-point unit.
Microcontrollers only support void pointers.
check.why: Strict aliasing rules in ISO C state that two pointers of different types cannot point to the same memory location. When code violates this rule with pointer casting, modern optimizing compilers (GCC/Clang) generate invalid machine code by reordering writes.

parts.title: Master Engine: MISRA-Compliant Fail-Safe Actuator Driver
say: We now synthesize all MISRA-C principles into an industrial-grade actuator driver.

Our driver enforces: 1) Strict essential types with 'U' literal suffixes; 2) Defensive parameter range validation; 3) Zero dynamic allocation; 4) Bounded iterative polling with finite timeouts; 5) Explicit status return codes with zero undefined behavior.
This architecture represents the exact standard required to pass an ISO 26262 ASIL-D functional safety audit in automotive firmware.
parts.example: A throttle valve actuator controller accepts target angles from 0 to 90 degrees. Inputs outside [0, 90] are rejected; movement loops are bounded by 1,000 timeout ticks; hardware status is checked without pointer punning.
parts.output:
--- DAY 28 PART 5: MISRA-COMPLIANT ACTUATOR ENGINE ---
[ACTUATOR-OK] Actuator reached target angle: 45 deg.
[ACTUATOR-FAULT] Commanded angle 120 exceeds MAX limit 90!
[ACTUATOR-OK] Actuator reached target angle: 0 deg.
[AUDIT-VERIFIED] Driver passes ISO 26262 ASIL-D defensive verification.

codeNotes.note: ActuatorStatus uses an explicit underlying type (uint32_t) and 'U' suffixes for complete determinism.
Defensive input validation rejects out-of-range values before arithmetic or mechanical operations take place.
Bounded loop ensures that a stalled motor or broken encoder cannot lock up the CPU core.

parts.tryIt: Add an assertion macro that logs file and line numbers to a non-volatile flash error log when an invalid angle is commanded.

check.question: What design characteristic ensures that the MisraActuatorDriver cannot cause a system-wide CPU deadlock?
options: The actuator slewing loop is strictly bounded by MAX_TIMEOUT_CYCLES, guaranteeing termination even if the mechanical motor stalls.
The driver disables the microcontroller NVIC interrupt controller.
The driver runs exclusively inside a high-priority interrupt service routine.
The driver allocates motor step commands dynamically using malloc().
check.why: By bounding every loop with a finite timeout counter, the driver guarantees that hardware failures (such as a seized motor shaft or severed encoder wire) result in a graceful error return rather than an infinite spinlock.

summary: In safety-critical systems, Undefined Behavior (UB) can cause optimizing compilers to delete essential safety checks.
MISRA-C:2012 eliminates language vulnerabilities through strict rules governing types, pointers, loops, and memory.
Rule 10.4 enforces Essential Types, eliminating implicit integer promotions and requiring explicit unsigned 'U' literals.
Rule 17.2 strictly bans recursion to ensure mathematical stack boundedness and prevent runtime stack exhaustion.
Rule 11.4 and Rule 21.3 forbid pointer punning and dynamic heap allocation, enforcing deterministic compile-time memory structures.

projectStep.title: Integrating Static Analysis Linters into the Firmware CI Pipeline
steps: Install Cppcheck and Clang-Tidy in the build environment.
Configure a rule deviation document justifying any unavoidable hardware register access exceptions.
Enforce a zero-warning threshold in the Git pre-commit hook to block non-compliant code from merging.
